content: Clear cell tumors are classified within the surface epithelial-stromal tumor group of ovarian cancers, representing approximately 6% of all ovarian neoplasms. These tumors are not exclusive to the ovaries and can also be associated with the pancreas and salivary glands. Benign and borderline variants of clear cell tumors are exceedingly rare, with the majority of cases being malignant. Morphologically, these tumors are typically cystic neoplasms characterized by polypoid masses that protrude into the cystic cavity. On microscopic pathological examination, clear cell tumors are composed of cells with clear cytoplasm, which contains glycogen. Additionally, they include hobnail cells, which are cells where the glycogen has been secreted. The architectural patterns of these tumors can vary and may present as glandular, papillary, or solid structures.
